message.content:
Below are some quick ways to pull out “detailed” information for a network interface on the two most common platforms.  
Feel free to pick the one that matches your environment (or let me know if you’re on something else).

---

## **Linux**

| What you want | Command | Why it’s useful |
|---------------|---------|-----------------|
| Basic status & MAC | `ip link show dev eth0` | Shows state (UP/DOWN), MTU, MAC, flags, etc. |
| Driver & firmware | `ethtool -i eth0` | Prints driver name, version, firmware, bus info. |
| Statistics counters | `ethtool -S eth0` | Lists per‑queue packet/byte counts, errors, collisions, etc. |
| Speed & duplex | `ethtool eth0 | grep -E 'Speed|Duplex'` | Current negotiated link speed and duplex mode. |
| Full hardware description | `lshw -class network -short` or `lshw -class network -numeric` | Gives vendor, product, physical location, capabilities. |
| Network configuration (addresses, routes) | `ip addr show dev eth0` | All IP addresses, prefixes, scope. |
| Routing table for that interface | `ip route show dev eth0` | Which routes are bound to this interface. |
| System logs for NIC events | `journalctl -u systemd-networkd.service --since today | grep eth0` | Recent link up/down events, DHCP leases, etc. |
| Raw sysfs data | `cat /sys/class/net/eth0/{address,speed,duplex,operstate}` | Low‑level attributes that other tools read. |

**Example usage**

```bash
$ ip link show dev eth0
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP mode DEFAULT group default qlen 1000
    link/ether 00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff

$ ethtool -i eth0
driver: e1000e
version: 3.2.6-k
firmware-version: 0.13-3
bus-info: 0000:03:00.0
supports-statistics: yes
supports-test: yes
supports-eeprom-access: yes
supports-register-dump: yes
supports-priv-flags: no

$ ethtool -S eth0 | head
rx_packets: 1234567
rx_bytes: 987654321
rx_errors: 0
rx_dropped: 0
```

---

## **Windows (PowerShell)**

| What you want | Cmdlet | Why it’s useful |
|---------------|--------|-----------------|
| Adapter properties | `Get-NetAdapter -Name "Ethernet" | Format-List *` | Full list of adapter settings, status, MAC, speed, etc. |
| IP configuration | `Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet"` | Addresses, DNS servers, gateway, DHCP status. |
| Detailed statistics | `Get-NetAdapterStatistics -Name "Ethernet"` | Packets sent/received, errors, collisions. |
| Driver info | `Get-NetAdapterAdvancedProperty -Name "Ethernet"` | Advanced settings exposed by the driver. |
| Event log entries | `Get-WinEvent -LogName System | Where-Object {$_.ProviderName -eq "Microsoft-Windows-NDIS"} | Where-Object {$_.Message -match "Ethernet"}` | Link up/down events, driver load/unload. |

**Example usage**

```powershell
PS C:\> Get-NetAdapter -Name "Ethernet" | Format-List *

Name              : Ethernet
InterfaceDescription : Intel(R) Ethernet Connection (2) I219-V
Status            : Up
MacAddress        : 00-1A-2B-3C-4D-5E
LinkSpeed         : 1 Gbps
...

PS C:\> Get-NetIPConfiguration -InterfaceAlias "Ethernet"

InterfaceAlias      : Ethernet
IPv4DefaultGateway  : 192.168.1.1
IPv4Address         : 192.168.1.42
...
```

---

### Quick sanity check

* If you’re on a **macOS** machine, replace the Linux commands with `ifconfig en0` or `networksetup -getinfo Ethernet`.
* If you’re dealing with a **virtual interface** (e.g., Docker bridge, VPN tunnel), the same Linux commands apply but the interface name will differ (`docker0`, `tun0`, etc.).

Let me know if you need help interpreting any of those outputs or if you’re on a different platform!
